metadata.name: [GCP Compute OTel] Persistent disk I/O saturation
metadata.description: Alerts when an attached disk has a sustained deep I/O queue (average queue depth >= 8) combined with elevated average I/O latency over 15 minutes, indicating it is at its IOPS or throughput ceiling. Latency thresholds differ by storage type. Returns one row per saturated disk.

data.content:
## Persistent disk I/O saturation

This disk has averaged a queue depth of at least 8 outstanding I/Os for 15 minutes while average I/O latency is also elevated. Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk performance is capped by disk type and size, so this pattern usually means the disk is at its IOPS or throughput limit and requests are queuing.

### Triage
1. Check read/write IOPS and throughput for the disk. A plateau at a constant level suggests the disk's performance cap has been reached.
2. Check `performance_status`. If latency is high but the queue is shallow, suspect infrastructure degradation rather than saturation (see the severely degraded disk rule).
3. Identify the workload: compactions, backups, log bursts, or batch jobs often cause temporary saturation.
4. `instance_name` is not available on these series; use `instance_id` (and the device name, which usually matches the VM name for boot disks) to find the VM.

### Remediation
Increase disk size (size-based PD performance scales with capacity), move to a faster disk type (pd-ssd, Hyperdisk), raise provisioned IOPS/throughput on Hyperdisk, or spread I/O across more disks or instances.

### Tuning
`queue_depth >= 8` and the per-storage-type `latency_threshold_ms` CASE (50 ms for pd-standard, 10 ms for others) are adjustable. GCP Cloud Monitoring metrics typically arrive several minutes late, so the most recent minutes of the lookback window may be empty; the window is sized to tolerate this.
